The Gulf of Tadjoura and the waters of the Bab-el-Mandeb strait make Djibouti a strategic port and refuelling point on one of the world's most important shipping routes between the Red Sea and Indian Ocean. Whale shark encounters in the Gulf of Tadjoura are internationally recognized for diving and snorkelling. The Lac Abbé saltflat landscape — featuring fumarole chimneys — has been used as a film location evoking extra-terrestrial terrain. Djibouti hosts several international military bases reflecting its strategic importance.
DMA: Dominica is internationally known as the 'Nature Isle of the Caribbean' — the island's volcanic terrain supports lush tropical rainforest, thermal springs, and the Boiling Lake (the world's second-largest boiling lake), distinguishing it from flatter Caribbean beach destinations. Dominica is internationally recognized in ecotourism and was selected as the world's first climate-resilient destination. The Kalinago (Carib) people, one of the Caribbean's surviving pre-Columbian indigenous communities, maintain traditional canoe carving and cultural practices on the island. Traditional Creole (Kokoy) language and cuisine — including callaloo, sancocho, and mountain chicken (a large frog) — are culturally distinctive.
DOM: The Dominican Republic is internationally associated with merengue and bachata music — both hold UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage status and have spread globally as popular dance music genres. Punta Cana and Samaná Peninsula are among the Caribbean's most internationally recognized beach and resort destinations. Baseball is the dominant sport, with the Dominican Republic producing the highest number of international MLB players per capita of any country. Dominican amber — containing prehistoric inclusions — is internationally traded and featured in Jurassic Park. Traditional Dominican cuisine includes la bandera (rice, beans, and meat), sancocho, and mangu (mashed plantains). The Santo Domingo Colonial Zone (UNESCO) is the oldest European city in the Americas.
ECU: Ecuador is internationally associated with the Galápagos Islands (UNESCO World Heritage Site) — the archipelago's extraordinary endemic wildlife (giant tortoises, marine iguanas, blue-footed boobies) inspired Charles Darwin's theory of natural selection during his 1835 visit and is internationally recognized in both science and conservation contexts. Ecuador is the world's largest exporter of premium roses, particularly from highland greenhouses near Quito. The Panama hat — a fine woven brimmed hat internationally associated with Panama — was traditionally made in Ecuador (particularly Montecristi and Cuenca). Ecuador is the world's top exporter of bananas. Ecuadorian cacao (Nacional variety) is internationally recognized as a fine-flavour chocolate source. The Inca heritage of Ingapirca is the country's most significant pre-Columbian site.
SLV: El Salvador is internationally associated with pupusas — thick handmade corn tortillas filled with cheese, beans, or chicharrón, recognized by UNESCO as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of El Salvador. The country's Pacific coast beaches attract a dedicated international surfing community, with spots including Punta Roca recognized in international surf competitions. El Salvador's Mayan heritage includes the Joya de Cerén archaeological site (UNESCO) — a pre-Columbian village preserved under volcanic ash, often called 'the Pompeii of the Americas.' Salvadoran cuisine also includes yuca frita, tamales, and sopa de pata. El Salvador became the world's first country to adopt Bitcoin as legal tender (2021). The mariposa (butterfly) tree blossom (Flor de Izote) is the national flower.
GNQ: Equatorial Guinea is internationally notable as the only Spanish-speaking country in sub-Saharan Africa. The country's mainland (Río Muni) and its islands, particularly Bioko Island (site of the capital Malabo), contain significant tropical rainforest ecosystems protecting populations of western lowland gorillas, chimpanzees, and drills. Equatorial Guinea became a significant oil producer following offshore discoveries in the 1990s. The country's Bwiti ceremonial tradition, shared with Gabon, involves the ritual use of iboga plant in initiation ceremonies. Traditional dance and music using drums, xylophones, and harps are culturally significant.
ERI: Eritrea is internationally associated with Asmara's exceptionally well-preserved Italian colonial modernist and Art Deco architecture — the capital city's built heritage has been described as 'Africa's secret modernist city' and received UNESCO World Heritage status in 2017. The Red Sea coast offers diving and snorkeling in relatively pristine coral reef environments. Traditional Eritrean coffee ceremony, incense burning, and injera-based communal meals (shared with Ethiopian traditions) are cultural practices. Camel caravan trade heritage crossing the Sahel and to the Red Sea coast reflects the country's historical position in East African and Arabian trade routes. Traditional music uses kirar (lyre) and krar instruments.
EST: Estonia is internationally recognized as a pioneer of digital governance — the country was the first in the world to offer e-residency (digital residency for non-citizens), and online voting, digital ID, and paperless government services are internationally referenced as models. Skype was founded in Estonia (2003). The Song Festival (Laulupidu, UNESCO Intangible Heritage) — a mass choral gathering dating to 1869 — played a significant role in the Singing Revolution that contributed to Estonia's independence from the Soviet Union in 1991. Tallinn's Medieval Old Town (UNESCO) features well-preserved Gothic and Hanseatic architecture. Baltic amber from Estonian coastal deposits is internationally traded. Traditional Estonian farm cuisine includes black rye bread, smoked fish, and kama.
SWZ: Eswatini is internationally associated with the Umhlanga (Reed Dance) ceremony — an annual gathering of tens of thousands of young Swazi women carrying reeds to present to the Queen Mother, an internationally recognized cultural spectacle. The Incwala (Kingship ceremony) is another internationally noted royal tradition. Eswatini is one of the world's few remaining absolute monarchies. Traditional Swazi craft traditions include coiled baskets, woodcarving, and beadwork. Hlane Royal National Park and Mlilwane Wildlife Sanctuary support rhino, elephant, and wildlife conservation programmes. Traditional Swazi cuisine includes sishwala (thick porridge) and emasi (fermented milk).
FLK: The Falkland Islands (Malvinas) is internationally associated with its subantarctic wildlife — large colonies of king penguins, rockhopper penguins, Magellanic penguins, black-browed albatross, elephant seals, and southern sea lions are found across the islands. The 1982 Falklands War between Argentina and the United Kingdom is a significant point of international historical reference. Sheep farming has historically been the economic foundation, and Falkland Islands wool is an export. Stanley is the capital. The islands are a departure point for Antarctic cruise expeditions. Wreck diving on 19th-century sailing ships sunk in the harbour is a recognized diving attraction.
FRO: The Faroe Islands is internationally recognized for its dramatic landscape — sheer sea cliffs, mountain plateaus rising from the North Atlantic, and puffin colonies create a distinctive scenery that has gained significant international photographic and travel attention. Traditional Faroese sheep farming on the steep island hillsides is the origin of the name ('Faroe' means Sheep Islands in Old Norse). The indigenous Faroese language, closely related to Old Norse and Icelandic, is spoken by the island's approximately 50,000 residents. Faroese music has gained international niche recognition through folk-fusion artists. Traditional chain dancing (DANS) is a UNESCO-recognized community tradition. The Faroe Islands is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.
FJI: Fiji is internationally associated with the traditional kava (yaqona) ceremony — the preparation and communal drinking of kava root extract is central to Fijian social and diplomatic hospitality and internationally recognized. Meke (traditional Fijian dance and storytelling performance) and lovo (underground oven feast) are recognized cultural traditions. Fiji's Bula! greeting is internationally associated with Fijian hospitality. Rugby sevens is internationally associated with Fiji — the national team has won Olympic gold medals and multiple World Rugby Sevens Series titles. Coral reef diving and tropical island landscapes (particularly in the Mamanuca and Yasawa groups) are internationally recognized tourism features. Fijian sulu (wraparound skirt) and traditional tapa cloth (masi) are recognized cultural items.
GUF: French Guiana is internationally associated with the Guiana Space Centre in Kourou — one of the world's most important rocket launch facilities, used by Ariane, Soyuz, and Vega rockets for commercial and scientific satellite launches. The site's proximity to the equator (approximately 5° North latitude) provides an orbital mechanics advantage that makes Kourou internationally preferred for equatorial satellite deployment. French Guiana's interior is covered by Amazon basin rainforest and home to Maroon communities — descendants of escaped enslaved people who established independent communities with distinct cultural traditions. The territory is an overseas department of France.
PYF: French Polynesia is internationally associated with Bora Bora's turquoise lagoon — one of the world's most recognized luxury travel destinations, associated with overwater bungalows (a concept first developed in French Polynesia in the late 1960s). Tahitian black pearls (poe rava) are internationally recognized premium jewellery items produced from black-lipped oysters cultivated in the Tuamotu and Gambier archipelagos. The French artist Paul Gauguin spent significant time in Tahiti and the Marquesas Islands in the 1890s and produced works that influenced the international art world. Traditional Polynesian navigation heritage — using stars, swells, and bird flight to cross vast Pacific distances — originated in the ancestral Polynesian homeland of Eastern Polynesia. Heiva festival celebrates traditional dance and outrigger canoe racing.
ATF: The French Southern and Antarctic Lands is internationally recognized as a group of remote subantarctic territories hosting some of the world's largest wildlife colonies — the Crozet Archipelago, Kerguelen Islands, and Amsterdam and St. Paul islands support enormous populations of king penguins, southern elephant seals, wandering albatross, and other subantarctic species. The Kerguelen Islands (Îles Désolation) are internationally associated with extreme remoteness. French scientific research stations operate on the islands year-round. The TAAF maritime exclusive economic zone is one of the world's largest.
GAB: Gabon is internationally recognized for its exceptional concentration of forest wildlife — the country has one of the highest densities of western lowland gorillas, forest elephants, and chimpanzees in Africa, supported by relatively intact rainforest (covering approximately 80% of land area). Lopé National Park (UNESCO) protects diverse habitats. The Bwiti spiritual ceremony — involving ritual use of the iboga plant root for initiation — is internationally recognized and has influenced ethnobotany and neuroscience research. Gabon is a significant oil producer. Leatherback sea turtles nest on Gabon's Atlantic beaches in globally significant numbers. Albert Schweitzer established a famous medical mission at Lambaréné.
GMB: The Gambia is internationally associated with bird-watching tourism — the country's location on the West African migration flyway and diverse riverine and coastal habitats attract international ornithologists. The Gambia River, the country's defining geographic feature, is navigable for most of its length through Gambia. Kunta Kinte, the enslaved African whose story was recounted in Alex Haley's novel Roots (and the subsequent television series), was from Juffureh village in Gambia, making the country internationally significant in African diaspora heritage tourism. Traditional Mandinka kora (21-string harp-lute) music is internationally recognized as a West African instrument. Baobab trees are iconic landscape features.
GEO: Georgia is internationally associated with wine — the country's Kvevri clay-vessel winemaking tradition (UNESCO Intangible Heritage) dates back approximately 8,000 years, making the South Caucasus region the world's oldest documented wine culture. Georgian polyphonic singing (UNESCO) is recognized as a distinctive three-voice choral tradition. The Cross of Saint Nino and the Georgian Apostolic Orthodox Church (established 4th century) are central to national identity. Tbilisi's diverse architectural heritage — Persian, Russian Imperial, Art Nouveau, and Soviet — creates a distinctive cityscape. Khachapuri (cheese bread in various regional styles), khinkali (dumplings), and chacha (grape marc spirit) are recognized Georgian culinary traditions. The Caucasus Mountain landscapes — including the Svaneti highlands and Kazbegi peaks — attract international trekking tourism.
GHA: Ghana is internationally associated with Kente cloth — a handwoven silk-and-cotton textile produced by Ashanti weavers in geometric patterns, adopted as a symbol of African heritage globally and worn in diaspora communities worldwide. Ghana was the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from colonial rule (1957), making it a significant symbol of African liberation. Highlife music, originating in Ghana and widely influencing West African popular music, and contemporary Afrobeats artists with Ghanaian roots are internationally recognized. Ghanaian cuisine includes fufu with groundnut soup, jollof rice, and kelewele. Elmina and Cape Coast castles (UNESCO) are internationally significant heritage sites related to the transatlantic slave trade. Kakum National Park's canopy walkway is a recognized ecotourism feature.
GIB: Gibraltar is internationally recognized for the Rock of Gibraltar — the massive limestone promontory at the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula guarding the Strait of Gibraltar between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. The Barbary macaques living semi-wild on the Upper Rock are internationally associated with Gibraltar, a legend holding that British sovereignty will last as long as the apes remain. Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory and a significant financial services and shipping hub. The Great Siege Tunnels (18th century) and the Moorish Castle reflect the site's long strategic history. The narrow Main Street shopping district has duty-free retail status.
GRL: Greenland is internationally associated with the world's largest island, covered approximately 80% by the Greenland Ice Sheet — the world's second-largest body of ice — which is internationally significant in climate science as a major indicator of global sea level change. Greenland's fjord landscapes, notably Ilulissat Icefjord (UNESCO), with calving glaciers producing enormous icebergs, are internationally photographed. The island is an autonomous territory of Denmark and home to the Inuit people (Kalaallit). The Northern Lights (aurora borealis) are reliably visible during long winter nights. Traditional Greenlandic kayak design (the qajaq) is the origin of the modern kayak. Greenlandic cuisine includes mattak (narwhal skin), muktuk, and dried fish.
GRD: Grenada is internationally associated with nutmeg production — the island produces approximately 20% of the world's supply, earning it the nickname 'Island of Spice.' The Spice Isle also exports mace, cloves, cinnamon, and cocoa. Grenada's cocoa, notably from the Belmont Estate, is internationally recognized in premium chocolate production circles. Grand Anse Beach is a prominently recognized Caribbean beach destination. The underwater sculpture park off Molinière Point — the world's first — is an internationally noted dive attraction. Grenada's annual Carriacou Parang Festival preserves Afro-Caribbean Christmas music traditions. Traditional oil-down (the national dish) and callaloo soup are recognized Grenadian culinary traditions.
GLP: Guadeloupe is internationally recognized as a French Caribbean overseas region consisting of two main islands — Basse-Terre and Grande-Terre — separated by the Rivière Salée strait. The active volcano La Soufrière on Basse-Terre and the Carbet Falls are significant natural landmarks. Guadeloupe has a distinctive Creole culture that blends French, African, and Caribbean traditions, expressed in gwo ka drumming and music (UNESCO). The Pointe-à-Pitre market is known for tropical produce and spice markets. Traditional Guadeloupean cuisine includes colombo (curry-influenced stew), accras (fritters), and ti punch (rum cocktail).
GUM: Guam is internationally recognized as the westernmost territory of the United States and a significant US military hub in the Western Pacific. Traditional Chamorro culture — indigenous to Guam and the Northern Marianas — includes latte stone pillars (ancient megalithic stone supports for houses), which are internationally recognized as a unique archaeological feature. The island is an international transit and tourism destination, particularly for visitors from Japan and South Korea. Liberation Day (July 21) commemorates liberation from Japanese occupation in 1944. Traditional Chamorro food includes kelaguen (citrus-marinated meat or fish), red rice, and coconut-based dishes.
GTM: Guatemala is internationally associated with the ancient Maya civilization — Tikal National Park (UNESCO dual World Heritage Site for both natural and cultural significance) features massive Classic Maya temple-pyramids rising above the rainforest canopy and is one of the most recognized archaeological sites in the Americas. Traditional Mayan weaving using backstrap looms — with complex symbolic patterns distinct to each community — is internationally collected and UNESCO-recognized. Antigua Guatemala (UNESCO) is a preserved colonial Spanish colonial city with distinctive baroque architecture and cobblestone streets. Lake Atitlán, surrounded by volcanoes, is internationally recognized for its dramatic landscape. Guatemalan coffee from the highlands is internationally traded in specialty markets. Quetzal (the national bird and currency name) is internationally symbolic.
GGY: Guernsey is internationally recognized as a British Crown dependency in the English Channel with a distinct Norman-French cultural heritage, expressed in Guernésiais (a Norman French dialect). The island has offshore financial services as a central economic activity. Victor Hugo spent much of his exile (1855–1870) in Guernsey, writing Les Misérables and other works at Hauteville House, which is internationally referenced. Guernsey cattle — a distinctive golden-brown dairy breed renowned for rich, high-butterfat milk — are internationally recognized and named after the island. Traditional Guernsey fishermen's jumpers (ganseys) influenced British maritime knitwear traditions.
GIN: Guinea is internationally associated with significant mineral wealth, particularly bauxite — the country has among the world's largest bauxite deposits, supplying a major share of global aluminium ore. The Fouta Djallon highland plateau, the source of major West African rivers including the Niger and Senegal rivers, is geographically significant. Traditional Guinean music — featuring the balafon, kora, and djembe drum — is central to Mande musical heritage and internationally recognized in West African music. Doura dance traditions and the griot oral storytelling tradition are significant cultural heritages. Guinean palm oil and red rice are traditional culinary foundations.
GNB: Guinea-Bissau is internationally recognized for its Bijagós Archipelago — a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve of approximately 90 islands with diverse mangrove, palm, and saltwater ecosystems, supporting one of the world's most significant saltwater hippopotamus populations and important sea turtle nesting beaches. The Bijagós people maintain matrilineal cultural traditions and distinctive initiation ceremonies. Guinea-Bissau's cashew nut production is among the largest per capita in the world, and cashew is the dominant export crop. Griot oral traditions, balafon music, and communal dance ceremonies are central cultural expressions.
GUY: Guyana is internationally associated with Kaieteur Falls — located in the Pakaraima Mountains in the interior rainforest, the falls drop approximately 226 metres in a single plunge, making it one of the world's most powerful waterfalls by volume and one of the most internationally recognized natural landmarks in South America. Guyana is the only English-speaking country in South America. The country's interior Amerindian communities (Wai Wai, Makushi, Patamona) maintain traditional forest-based cultural practices. The Rupununi savanna hosts giant anteaters, giant river otters, and diverse wildlife. Guyanese cuisine includes pepperpot (a spiced meat stew), cook-up rice, and black cake.
HTI: Haiti is internationally recognized as the site of the Haitian Revolution (1791–1804) — the only successful slave revolution in history, producing the world's first Black republic and the first Latin American country to gain independence. The Citadelle Laferrière fortress (UNESCO, with the Sans-Souci Palace), built by Henri Christophe in the early 19th century, is an internationally recognized monument to Haitian independence and a remarkable engineering achievement. Haitian Vodou (a syncretic spiritual tradition blending African religious practices with Catholic elements) has international cultural influence. Haitian naïve art painting and metal sculpture crafts are internationally collected art traditions. Traditional Haitian cuisine includes griot (fried pork), diri kole ak pwa (rice and beans), and akasan porridge.
HMD: Heard Island and McDonald Islands is internationally recognized as an Australian external territory in the subantarctic Indian Ocean. It contains two active volcanoes — Big Ben on Heard Island is one of Australia's two active volcanoes. The islands are UNESCO-listed for their pristine subantarctic ecosystem — untouched by introduced species and supporting large colonies of macaroni, king, and gentoo penguins, elephant seals, and southern fur seals. The territory is extremely remote and uninhabited.
HND: Honduras is internationally associated with the Maya archaeological site of Copán (UNESCO World Heritage Site) — its elaborately carved stelae, hieroglyphic stairway, and altar sculptures represent the artistic and scholarly peak of Maya civilization. The Bay Islands, particularly Roatán, are internationally recognized diving destinations on the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef, the world's second-largest coral reef system. Honduran coffee from the highlands is internationally traded in specialty markets. The Garífuna communities on the Caribbean coast — descendants of Afro-Caribbean and Arawak peoples — maintain UNESCO-recognized music, dance, and language traditions. Baleadas (flour tortillas with beans) are the most widely recognized Honduran everyday food.
HKG: Hong Kong is internationally associated with its dramatic skyline — one of the world's most photographed urban landscapes, featuring dense high-rise towers along Victoria Harbour, with Victoria Peak viewpoints internationally recognized. Dim sum (yum cha) culture — the tradition of communal morning or midday meals of small bamboo-steamed dishes — is internationally recognized and has spread globally through diaspora communities. Hong Kong cinema, particularly martial arts films and the work of directors John Woo and Wong Kar-wai, and actors Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan, are internationally influential. The Mid-Autumn Festival lantern traditions and Dragon Boat racing are recognized cultural events. Cha chaan teng (Hong Kong-style tea restaurants) and egg tarts (dan tat) are associated internationally with Hong Kong food culture.
IRQ: Iraq is internationally associated with Mesopotamia — the 'Land Between the Rivers' (Tigris and Euphrates) is widely identified as one of the cradles of civilization, where Sumer, Akkad, Babylon, and Assyria developed writing (cuneiform), codified law (Hammurabi), urban planning, and early agriculture. The ancient cities of Babylon, Uruk, Ur, and Nineveh represent globally significant archaeological heritage. Traditional Iraqi music using the oud lute and maqam (classical melodic modes) is internationally recognized. The ziggurat of Ur, the Ishtar Gate, and the ancient market cities of the Silk Road are internationally referenced in history and archaeology. Mesopotamian date palms and Iraqi date production have ancient heritage recognition.
IRL: Ireland is internationally associated with its diaspora — approximately 70–80 million people worldwide claim Irish heritage (compared to a resident population of approximately 5 million), making the Irish diaspora one of the most historically significant in the world. Traditional Irish music (uilleann pipes, fiddle, tin whistle, bodhrán drum) is internationally recognized, and sessions in public houses (pubs) have spread globally. Guinness stout, brewed in Dublin since 1759, is one of the world's most recognized beer brands. The Cliffs of Moher, Ring of Kerry, and Giant's Causeway are internationally recognized landscape destinations. Literature — James Joyce, William Butler Yeats, Samuel Beckett, Oscar Wilde, and George Bernard Shaw — has given Ireland an outsized international literary reputation. Traditional Irish soda bread and Irish stew are recognized foods.
IMN: The Isle of Man is internationally known for the TT (Tourist Trophy) motorcycle races — held on public roads around the island circuit since 1907, the races are internationally recognized as among the world's most challenging and prestigious motorcycle racing events. The island is a British Crown dependency with its own parliament (Tynwald, established c. 979 AD, claimed as the world's oldest continuous parliament). Offshore financial services are a significant economic activity. Manx Loaghtan sheep (with four or six horns) and Manx cats (known for their taillessness) are internationally associated breeds. The island's Celtic heritage is expressed in the Manx Gaelic language, which has been subject to revitalization efforts.
JEY: Jersey is a British Crown dependency in the English Channel known for Jersey cattle — a distinctive small dairy breed internationally recognized for high-fat, golden milk — and Jersey Royal potatoes, which have Protected Designation of Origin status and are internationally recognized as a premium early new potato variety. Offshore financial services, particularly in trust and private banking, are a central economic activity. The island's Norman French cultural heritage is reflected in Jèrriais (a Norman dialect). Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust, founded by author Gerald Durrell in Jersey, is internationally recognized in conservation and captive breeding.
JOR: Jordan is internationally associated with Petra (UNESCO World Heritage Site, one of the New Seven Wonders of the World) — the rose-red Nabataean city carved into sandstone cliffs, including the Treasury (Al-Khazneh) facade, is one of the world's most photographed and internationally recognized archaeological landmarks. The Dead Sea, the lowest point on Earth's surface, is internationally recognized as a unique natural body of water where the extremely high salinity allows effortless floating. Wadi Rum's desert landscape — vast red-sand valleys with towering sandstone formations — is internationally recognized and has served as a filming location for numerous international productions. Traditional Jordanian cuisine includes mansaf (lamb slow-cooked in fermented dried yogurt sauce, the national dish), falafel, and knafeh.
KAZ: Kazakhstan is internationally associated with the Baikonur Cosmodrome — the world's first and largest operational space launch facility, from which Sputnik (1957), Yuri Gagarin's flight (1961), and numerous subsequent space missions were launched, making it internationally significant in the history of space exploration. The vast Kazakh steppe is associated with nomadic horse culture — Kazakhs are internationally associated with the tradition of eagle hunting (berkutchi, UNESCO Intangible Heritage), and kumiss (fermented mare's milk) is a traditional beverage. Kazakh yurt (shanyrak) architecture and carpet-weaving traditions are recognized crafts. The ancient Silk Road cities of Taraz and Turkestan are part of Kazakhstan's historical heritage. Beshbarmak (boiled meat on flat noodles) is the traditional national dish.
KIR: Kiribati (pronounced 'Kiribas') is internationally recognized for its position on the front lines of climate change — many of its 33 low-lying atolls sit only 1–2 metres above sea level, and the country faces existential risk from rising sea levels, making it globally significant in international climate change discussions. Kiribati straddles both the equator and the International Date Line. Traditional Kiribati canoe navigating traditions and I-Kiribati dance (including the te bino standing dance) are recognized cultural practices. Kiribati was the site of significant Pacific Island battles during World War II, particularly on Tarawa. The Phoenix Islands Protected Area (UNESCO) is one of the world's largest marine protected areas.
UNK: Kosovo is internationally recognized for its rich early Christian and Byzantine heritage — the medieval monasteries of Visoki Dečani, Patriarchate of Peć, and Gračanica (all UNESCO World Heritage Sites) feature exceptional Byzantine fresco painting. The Kosovo Polje battlefield (1389) is a foundational event in Serbian medieval history and cultural memory. Pristina, the capital, is a young, growing city with a notable café culture and informal commercial energy. Traditional Kosovo Albanian embroidery and silver filigree jewellery are recognized crafts. Flija (layered pastry cooked over embers) and qebapa (grilled sausages) are among the recognized traditional foods. Kosovo declared independence in 2008 and is recognized by approximately 100 countries.
KWT: Kuwait is internationally associated with its petroleum heritage — the discovery of oil at Burgan Field (1938), one of the world's largest oil fields, transformed the country and drove Kuwait's emergence as one of the world's wealthiest per-capita nations. The Kuwaiti dhow maritime tradition and pearl diving heritage predate the oil era. The Kuwait Towers (completed 1979) are internationally recognized architectural symbols of the country. The Al Qurain Martyrs' Museum and Liberation Day reflect the national memory of the Gulf War (1990–91) Iraqi occupation and liberation. Traditional Kuwaiti cuisine includes machboos (spiced rice with meat), harees (wheat porridge), and muhallabia (milk pudding).
KGZ: Kyrgyzstan is internationally associated with the Tian Shan mountains — the country's high-altitude landscape includes the spectacular Son-Kul and Issyk-Kul lakes (Issyk-Kul being one of the world's largest alpine lakes), yurt camps, and nomadic herding traditions. Kyrgyz yurt (boz üy) construction and felt-craft traditions — including shyrdak (felt rugs) and ala-kiyiz, are UNESCO Intangible Heritage crafts. Traditional eagle hunting (UNESCO) is practiced in Kyrgyzstan's mountain regions. The Epic of Manas — the world's longest oral epic poem, with over 500,000 lines — is central to Kyrgyz cultural identity. Kumiss (fermented mare's milk) and beshbarmak (meat and noodle dish) are traditional foods.
LAO: Laos is internationally associated with the serene town of Luang Prabang (UNESCO World Heritage Site) — noted for its exceptional blend of French colonial architecture and traditional Lao wooden temple (wat) structures along the Mekong River, and the daily alms-giving ceremony (tak bat) in which monks in saffron robes collect food from residents at dawn. The Plain of Jars archaeological site — featuring thousands of stone jars of unknown origin scattered across the plateau — is internationally intriguing and UNESCO-listed. Lao cuisine includes larb (minced meat salad), sticky rice (khao niao, a Lao staple), and Beerlao, the national beer internationally distributed. Laos has more unexploded ordnance per capita than any country from the Vietnam War era, an internationally noted humanitarian issue.
LVA: Latvia is internationally associated with the Latvian Song and Dance Festival (Dziesmu un Deju svētki, UNESCO Intangible Heritage) — a mass gathering dating to 1873 in which tens of thousands of singers and dancers perform traditional Latvian folk repertoire, and which played a significant role in the Singing Revolution (1987–1991). Latvian amber from the Baltic coast — known as Baltic gold — is internationally traded as a gemstone and is among the world's most significant amber deposit regions. Riga's Art Nouveau architecture (UNESCO) — one of Europe's finest concentrations — is internationally recognized, with approximately one-third of the city centre's buildings in the style. Traditional Latvian rye bread (rupjmaize) and grey peas (pelēkie zirņi) are recognized national foods.
LBN: Lebanon is internationally associated with its cuisine — Levantine food including hummus, baba ghanoush, tabbouleh, kibbeh, fattoush, and mezze spreads are globally recognized as 'Lebanese' food, internationally spread through diaspora communities across South America, West Africa, and Australia. Cedar of Lebanon — the tree on the national flag — was historically one of the most prized building materials in the ancient world (used in Solomon's Temple and Egyptian ships). The Phoenician civilization, originating in the coastal cities of Byblos, Sidon, and Tyre (UNESCO), is credited with developing one of the world's earliest alphabets. Baalbek's Roman temples (UNESCO) are among the best-preserved and most monumental in the world. Beirut is internationally known for its vibrant arts, nightlife, and publishing scene.
LSO: Lesotho is internationally notable as one of only three countries entirely surrounded by a single other country (South Africa), and as the highest country in the world by lowest-point elevation (above 1,400 metres). The Maloti-Drakensberg Park (UNESCO, shared with South Africa) features dramatic basalt mountain scenery and San Bushmen rock art. Traditional Basotho culture is represented by the distinctive Basotho blanket (a woollen blanket worn as a cloak, used as outerwear and in ceremonies) and conical woven Basotho hat (mokorotlo, depicted on the national flag). Pony trekking through the highlands on Basotho ponies is an internationally recognized Lesotho tourism experience. Traditional sorghum beer is a cultural staple.
LBR: Liberia is internationally noted as the first African republic to proclaim independence (1847), established largely by freed American and Caribbean enslaved people, and as Africa's oldest republic. The country's capital, Monrovia, is named after US President James Monroe. Traditional Liberian music includes the Kpanlogo and various Mande music traditions. Liberia's maritime flag of convenience (ship registry) is among the world's largest, with thousands of international vessels registered under the Liberian flag. The country's Atlantic coastline fishing culture and palm oil traditions are historically significant. Liberian pepper, particularly the Grains of Paradise (melegueta pepper), was historically traded to Europe.
LBY: Libya is internationally associated with the ancient Greco-Roman cities of Cyrene (UNESCO) and Leptis Magna (UNESCO) — Leptis Magna in particular is considered one of the best-preserved Roman cities in the world, with magnificent amphitheatres, temples, and market buildings largely intact in the Saharan desert. The Sahara Desert covers the majority of Libya's territory and contains the Akakus rock art formations (UNESCO). Libya has some of the world's largest proven oil reserves. Traditional Libyan cuisine includes bazeen (hard barley dough with meat), shakshouka, and couscous. The ancient caravan routes crossing the Libyan Sahara were significant in trans-Saharan trade history.
LIE: Liechtenstein is internationally associated with being one of the world's wealthiest per-capita countries, with a highly developed financial services sector (notably private banking and business registration) and low-tax status attracting a high density of registered corporations. It is one of only two doubly landlocked countries in the world (entirely surrounded by other landlocked countries — Switzerland and Austria). The Prince of Liechtenstein owns one of the world's largest private art collections (the Liechtenstein Museum collection). Traditional Liechtenstein wine production from Rhine Valley vineyards and skiing at Malbun resort are recognized local activities. The country abolished its army in 1868 after the Austro-Prussian War.
LTU: Lithuania is internationally associated with the Baltic amber trade — along with Latvia and Estonia, Lithuania's amber coast has supplied amber to Europe and the Mediterranean for thousands of years, and Baltic amber with prehistoric inclusions (insects, plant matter) is internationally studied. The Hill of Crosses (Kryžių kalnas) near Šiauliai — a site of over 100,000 crosses planted by Catholic pilgrims over centuries, especially during Soviet occupation — is internationally recognized as a powerful symbol of faith and peaceful resistance. Vilnius Old Town (UNESCO) features outstanding Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque architecture. Lithuania's basketball programme is internationally recognized — the country has produced multiple NBA players relative to its population. Rye bread and cepelinai (potato dumplings stuffed with meat, UNESCO-listed) are recognized foods.
LUX: Luxembourg is internationally recognized as one of Europe's wealthiest and most financially significant countries — the Grand Duchy hosts a disproportionately large number of European institutions (European Court of Justice, Court of Auditors, Eurostat), major investment fund administration, and private banking operations. The fortified old town and fortifications of Luxembourg City (UNESCO) reflect centuries of strategic significance, earning the city the title 'Gibraltar of the North.' The Moselle Valley wine region produces internationally known Riesling and Crémant de Luxembourg wines. Lëtzebuergesch (Luxembourgish) is the national language — a Germanic language distinct from German and French. Judd mat Gaardebounen (smoked collar of pork with broad beans) is the recognized national dish.
MAC: Macau is internationally associated with its casino industry — the Special Administrative Region of China overtook Las Vegas in total gaming revenue in 2006 and became the world's largest gambling destination by revenue. The Historic Centre of Macau (UNESCO) blends Portuguese colonial Baroque architecture with Chinese temples, reflecting Macau's history as a Portuguese territory from 1557 to 1999 and the resulting unique Luso-Chinese cultural fusion. Pastéis de nata (Portuguese egg tarts, called dan tat) have become internationally associated with Macau and spread throughout Asia. Macanese cuisine is a recognized fusion of Portuguese and Chinese cooking traditions. Macau was the gateway for the first sustained European commercial presence in East Asia.
MDG: Madagascar is internationally associated with its exceptional biodiversity — approximately 90% of Madagascar's wildlife is found nowhere else on Earth, including all five families of lemurs (over 100 species), the fossa predator, and extraordinary endemic plant communities. The baobab alley (Avenue of the Baobabs near Morondava) — ancient giant trees silhouetted against sunset skies — is one of Africa's most internationally recognized landscape photographs. The Tsingy de Bemaraha (UNESCO) — a UNESCO World Heritage Site featuring extraordinary limestone needle formations — is internationally cited as one of Africa's most spectacular geological sites. Traditional Malagasy silk weaving (lamba) and tomb construction culture are recognized cultural practices. Vanilla from Madagascar is the world's primary source.
MWI: Malawi is internationally associated with Lake Malawi (UNESCO) — the 'Lake of Stars,' the world's ninth-largest lake, containing the world's greatest diversity of freshwater fish (over 700 cichlid species, more than half found nowhere else). The warm lake water and fish diversity attract international diving and snorkeling tourism. Malawi is internationally recognized for its lake fishing culture — the chambo cichlid is a traditional dietary staple. Traditional Malawian music includes Gule Wamkulu (a masked ceremonial dance, UNESCO Intangible Heritage) performed by the Chewa people. Malawi tea from the Shire Highlands is internationally traded, and tobacco has historically been a significant export crop.
MDV: The Maldives is internationally recognized as a luxury overwater bungalow destination — the concept of positioning resort villas directly over the lagoon on stilts, with glass floors or staircases to the reef below, was pioneered and most associated globally with the Maldives. The country is entirely low-lying, with an average elevation of approximately 1.5 metres above sea level, making it internationally cited as one of the nations most immediately threatened by sea-level rise. The Maldivian coral reef ecosystem is among the world's most biodiverse for marine life. Traditional Maldivian dhoni boat design is internationally recognized. Maldivian cuisine centres on tuna (skipjack tuna is the staple fish) in dishes such as garudhiya soup and mas riha.
MLI: Mali is internationally associated with Timbuktu (UNESCO) — the historic scholarly city and trans-Saharan trade hub containing mosques (Djinguereber, Sankore) and manuscript collections representing the golden age of Islamic scholarship in 14th–15th century West Africa. The Djenné mosque (UNESCO, annually replastered in a communal ceremony) is the world's largest mud-brick building and internationally recognized as an extraordinary architectural achievement. The Mali Empire (13th–16th centuries) was one of the largest and wealthiest empires in history, and Mansa Musa's 1324 pilgrimage to Mecca, distributing gold along the way, became internationally legendary. Traditional Malian music — kora, balafon, and Mandinka griot traditions — is internationally recognized. The Dogon people's ritual mask dances and cosmological tradition are internationally studied.
MLT: Malta is internationally associated with ancient megalithic temples (UNESCO) — the Ħaġar Qim, Mnajdra, and Ġgantija temples predate Stonehenge and the Egyptian pyramids and represent the world's oldest free-standing stone architecture, dating to approximately 3600–2500 BCE. Valletta, the world's smallest capital by area (UNESCO World Heritage City), is internationally recognized for its Baroque architecture, built by the Knights of St. John. The Maltese Falcon (associated with the 1941 film) and the Maltese Cross have given Malta international symbolic recognition. Malta's role in World War II — awarded the George Cross by King George VI for collective bravery under siege — is historically significant. The Maltese language is the only Semitic language written in the Latin script and is the official language of the EU from a Semitic root.
MHL: The Marshall Islands is internationally known for the Bikini Atoll (UNESCO World Heritage Site) — where the United States conducted 23 nuclear weapons tests between 1946 and 1958, including the first hydrogen bomb (Castle Bravo, 1954), making it an internationally significant site in Cold War and nuclear history. The islands are among the nations most threatened by sea-level rise, with many atolls sitting barely above sea level. Traditional Marshallese stick chart navigation — maps made from coconut palm ribs and cowrie shells representing wave patterns between islands — is an internationally recognized example of indigenous Pacific navigation knowledge. The Bikini Atoll lagoon is a recognized diving destination.
MTQ: Martinique is internationally recognized as the birthplace of Empress Joséphine de Beauharnais (1763–1814), wife of Napoleon Bonaparte. The island's cultural heritage blends French, African, and Creole traditions, expressed in the zouk music genre (which emerged in Martinique and Guadeloupe in the 1980s and spread internationally). Mount Pelée is a historically active stratovolcano — its 1902 eruption destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre and killed approximately 30,000 people in one of the deadliest volcanic events of the 20th century. Martinique is internationally recognized for its rum agricole production, particularly from the Rhum Clément and Depaz distilleries. The island holds Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée status for rum agricole from fresh sugarcane juice.
MRT: Mauritania is internationally associated with the ancient Saharan caravan city of Chinguetti (UNESCO) — a centre of Islamic scholarship and pilgrimage in the Western Sahara, once considered the seventh holiest city in Islam, and its ancient manuscript libraries are recognized cultural heritage. The country's northern Sahara features dramatic erg (sand sea) landscapes, including Erg Amatlich. Traditional Moorish culture — including tent-dwelling nomadic heritage, Arabic-Hassaniya dialect, and green tea ceremony (ataya, prepared in three rounds of progressively sweeter glasses) — is culturally central. Mauritanian iron ore from Zouerate is transported by the world's longest trains (sometimes exceeding 2 kilometres in length) to Nouadhibou port.
MUS: Mauritius is internationally associated with the dodo — the flightless bird (Raphus cucullatus) endemic to Mauritius that became extinct in the late 17th century following human settlement and is an internationally recognized symbol of extinction and conservation responsibility. Mauritius is also widely cited for its economic development model — a small island that transitioned from monocrop sugar production to a diversified economy combining tourism, financial services, and technology within decades. The island is internationally recognized as a luxury beach resort destination, particularly Le Morne Brabant (UNESCO). Creole Mauritian cuisine blends Indian, French, Chinese, and African influences, including rougaille, dholl puri, and octopus curry. Sugar cane rum (Green Island, Pink Pigeon) is an export.
MYT: Mayotte is internationally associated with its marine lagoon — one of the world's largest closed lagoons, ringed by a double barrier reef — and its concentration of nesting green sea turtles and humpback whale calving activity, making it an internationally recognized marine ecotourism destination. The island is a French overseas department in the Indian Ocean near Madagascar. Comorian and Mahorais cultural traditions, Swahili influences, and traditional ylang-ylang perfume flower cultivation are cultural features. Traditional pirogues (outrigger canoes) are used for lagoon fishing.
FSM: The Federated States of Micronesia is internationally associated with Nan Madol (UNESCO World Heritage Site) on Pohnpei island — a series of small artificial islands constructed from basalt logs forming a ruined Saudeleur dynasty ceremonial centre, sometimes called the 'Venice of the Pacific.' The Yap islands within FSM are known for Rai — enormous stone discs used as traditional currency, which are internationally recognized as a distinctive form of monetary exchange. Traditional stick navigation charts and canoe sailing traditions are recognized Pacific heritage practices. The Caroline Islands' marine ecosystems, including diving at Truk (Chuuk) Lagoon — one of the world's premier wreck diving sites — are internationally recognized.
MDA: Moldova is internationally associated with wine production — the country has one of the world's highest per-capita vineyard areas and is home to the Mileștii Mici winery, which holds the Guinness record for the world's largest wine collection by number of bottles (approximately 1.5 million). The Cricova winery underground cellar network, used as a wine museum and storage facility, is internationally known. Traditional Moldovan cuisine includes mămăligă (polenta-like cornmeal porridge), sarmale (stuffed vine leaves), and plăcinte (pastries). Moldovan folk music, particularly the doina lyrical tradition, and hora circle dance are recognized cultural practices. The Orheiul Vechi cave monastery complex carved into limestone cliffs above the Răut river is a significant heritage site.
MCO: Monaco is internationally associated with the Monaco Grand Prix — the Formula One street circuit race through the narrow roads and tunnels of the principality, considered one of the most challenging and glamorous races on the F1 calendar. Monte Carlo Casino (opened 1863) is internationally recognized as a symbol of luxury gambling and has appeared in numerous internationally known films (including James Bond films). Monaco is the world's most densely populated sovereign state. The Prince of Monaco (Grimaldi family since 1297) makes it one of the world's oldest ruling dynasties. The Monaco Oceanographic Museum (directed by Jacques Cousteau 1957–1988) is internationally recognized in marine science. Monaco has no income tax.
MNG: Mongolia is internationally associated with Genghis Khan and the Mongol Empire (13th–14th centuries) — the largest contiguous land empire in history, stretching from the Pacific Ocean to Eastern Europe and profoundly shaping the history of Eurasia. Traditional nomadic pastoral culture — living in portable felt gers (yurts), horsemanship, eagle hunting (UNESCO), and Naadam festival (UNESCO, featuring horse racing, wrestling, and archery) — is internationally recognized as Mongolia's living heritage. Mongolian throat singing (khoomei, UNESCO) — producing multiple tones simultaneously — is an internationally recognized and studied vocal tradition. Mongolia's vast steppe landscape, Gobi Desert, and Mongolian horse traditions are internationally recognized in travel and cultural contexts. Airag (fermented mare's milk) and horhog (stone-cooked meat) are traditional foods.
MNE: Montenegro is internationally recognized for its dramatic concentration of coastline, fjords, and mountains within a small area — the Bay of Kotor (UNESCO) features a fjord-like deep bay ringed by dramatic limestone karst mountains and medieval Venetian walled towns, making it one of Europe's most recognized scenic coastal landscapes. The name Montenegro means 'Black Mountain' in Italian. Durmitor National Park (UNESCO) features glacial lakes and deep canyons including Tara Canyon, one of Europe's deepest. Montenegro was the first country in the world to officially declare its environmental neutrality by constitution. Traditional rakija (fruit brandy) and njeguški pršut (smoked Njeguški ham) are internationally associated with Montenegrin food culture.
MSR: Montserrat is internationally recognized for the Soufrière Hills volcanic eruption that began in 1995 — the eruption buried Plymouth (the capital) in pyroclastic flow deposits, creating a 'Caribbean Pompeii' visible in the exclusion zone and making it one of the most internationally referenced active volcano events of the late 20th century. Montserrat has a deep music heritage — Arrow, who created the calypso standard 'Hot Hot Hot,' was Montserratian, and George Martin's AIR Studios was located on the island (recording the Rolling Stones, Paul McCartney, and others) before the volcano erupted. The island is a British Overseas Territory.
MOZ: Mozambique is internationally associated with its long Indian Ocean coastline — stretching over 2,500 kilometres with coral reefs, mangroves, and offshore islands including the Bazaruto Archipelago (a marine national park) internationally recognized for dugong conservation and pristine dive sites. The island of Mozambique (Ilha de Moçambique, UNESCO) — a former Portuguese colonial capital with Swahili, Arab, and Portuguese architectural layers — is internationally recognized for its heritage. Marrabenta music is a traditional urban Mozambican popular music genre. Mozambican cuisine features piri piri prawns (camarão à piri piri), xima (maize porridge), and matapa (cassava leaves with coconut).
MMR: Myanmar (Burma) is internationally associated with Shwedagon Pagoda in Yangon — a 98-metre-tall gilded stupa reputedly containing relics of four Buddhas, one of Buddhism's most sacred and internationally recognized religious monuments. The ancient temple city of Bagan — with over 2,200 surviving Buddhist temples and stupas spread across a vast plain — is internationally recognized as one of Asia's most extraordinary archaeological landscapes (UNESCO). Burmese marionette theatre (yama zatdaw) and Mandalay classical dance drama are UNESCO Intangible Heritage traditions. Lacquerware production from Bagan and Mandalay is internationally recognized as a craft tradition. Mohinga (fish noodle soup) is widely considered Myanmar's national breakfast dish. Longyi (wraparound skirt-like garment worn by both men and women) is internationally recognized as Myanmar's national dress.
NAM: Namibia is internationally associated with the Namib Desert — one of the world's oldest deserts and the source of the country's name, its star dunes at Sossusvlei (particularly the photogenic Dune 45 and Deadvlei salt pan with dead camel-thorn trees) are among the world's most internationally reproduced landscape images. Etosha National Park is internationally recognized for wildlife, particularly large lion prides, rhinos, and desert-adapted elephants. Namibia was the first country in the world to incorporate environmental protection into its constitution. The Himba people — semi-nomadic pastoralists who use otjize (red ochre and butterfat paste) in their traditional appearance — are internationally recognized as a cultural group. Traditional San Bushmen rock engravings at Twyfelfontein (UNESCO) are internationally significant.
NRU: Nauru is internationally recognized as the world's smallest island nation (approximately 21 square kilometres) and the world's smallest republic. It was historically one of the world's wealthiest per-capita countries due to phosphate mining that lasted until reserves were largely exhausted. The island's landscape shows significant excavation from phosphate extraction. Nauru currently operates one of the Pacific's largest offshore banking and asset management sectors. The island's community has internationally recognized challenges in transitioning economically after phosphate depletion.
NPL: Nepal is internationally associated with Mount Everest (Sagarmatha) — the world's highest peak (8,849 metres), known in Nepali as Sagarmatha, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Nepal is home to eight of the world's ten highest mountains, making it the global centre for high-altitude mountaineering. The Kathmandu Valley's sacred architectural heritage — including Pashupatinath temple (UNESCO), Boudhanath stupa (UNESCO, one of the world's largest Buddhist stupas), and Swayambhunath (Monkey Temple) — is internationally recognized. Traditional Sherpa culture and high-altitude expertise are internationally associated with Nepal. Thangka painting and Buddhist mandala art are internationally collected Nepali artistic traditions. Traditional Nepali dal bhat (lentils and rice) and momo (dumplings) are recognized foods.
NCL: New Caledonia is internationally associated with its exceptional biodiversity and lagoon ecosystem (UNESCO) — the New Caledonian lagoon is the world's largest enclosed lagoon and has been recognized as the world's largest UNESCO marine World Heritage Site, containing remarkable coral reef biodiversity. The kagu bird — a nearly flightless, silvery-white bird endemic to New Caledonia — is the national symbol and internationally recognized in ornithology. New Caledonia is the world's second or third largest nickel producer. The indigenous Kanak people maintain traditional kastom (custom) ceremonies, architecture, and weaving traditions. Bougna (traditional Kanak earth-oven feast with taro, yam, and seafood in banana leaf) is a recognized cultural food tradition.
NIC: Nicaragua is internationally associated with the two large lakes — Lake Nicaragua (Cocibolca), which is the largest lake in Central America, and contains the world's only freshwater sharks (bull sharks adapted to freshwater), and Lake Managua. The colonial city of Granada on Lake Nicaragua is internationally recognized as one of the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded cities in the Americas. Nicaragua's Pacific-facing volcanoes — Masaya (with an accessible active lava lake), Momotombo, and the Concepción and Maderas twin peaks on Ometepe island — are internationally recognized landscape features. Nicaraguan rum (Flor de Caña) is an internationally distributed premium product. Traditional textiles from Masaya are recognized craft outputs.
NER: Niger is internationally associated with the Aïr Mountains and the Sahara — the Aïr and Ténéré Natural Reserves (UNESCO) protect extraordinary Saharan desert and mountain landscapes with prehistoric rock art, ancient trans-Saharan trade routes, and semi-nomadic Tuareg communities. The Tuareg people — Berber nomadic pastoralists of the Sahara — are internationally recognized for their traditional culture, silver jewellery, indigo clothing, and camel caravans. Niger has significant uranium deposits and is among the world's top uranium producers. Traditional architecture of the mud-walled old city of Agadez (UNESCO), including the iconic mosque minaret, is internationally recognized. The Cure Salée (salt cure) festival celebrating Tuareg and Wodaabe pastoralist cultures is internationally noted.
NIU: Niue is internationally recognized as one of the world's largest coral islands (as opposed to low-lying atolls) and one of the most isolated inhabited islands in the Pacific, with a population that has significantly decreased through emigration to New Zealand. The island is internationally noted for its exceptional marine environment — crystal-clear water, sea caves (talava arches), and spinner dolphin activity attract diving tourism. Niue was the world's first country to offer free wireless internet access to all residents. The Huvalu Community Conservation Area protects inland tropical forest. Niue is in free association with New Zealand.
NFK: Norfolk Island is an Australian external territory in the South Pacific internationally recognized for its two layers of heritage: the remains of the Kingston and Arthur's Vale Historic Area (UNESCO) from the brutal British penal colony period (1788–1856), and the community of descendants of the Bounty mutineers (from Pitcairn Island, relocated to Norfolk in 1856). The Norfolk Pine tree — a distinctive tall, symmetrical conifer — is internationally recognized as an architectural and botanical feature of the island's landscape. The Pitcairn-Norfolk language, a creole combining 18th-century English and Tahitian, is still spoken.
PRK: North Korea (DPRK) is internationally associated with its highly distinctive visual culture of monumental statuary, revolutionary art, and mass spectacle — the Arirang Mass Games (Grand Mass Gymnastics and Artistic Performance), featuring tens of thousands of synchronized performers, are internationally recognized as a uniquely spectacular public cultural event. The ancient Goguryeo Kingdom (37 BCE–668 CE) tombs with painted murals (UNESCO) represent significant early Korean cultural heritage shared with the Korean peninsula. Traditional Korean cuisine elements — including kimchi fermentation and bibimbap — predate the division. Paektu Mountain (Mt. Baekdu), the highest peak on the Korean peninsula and a sacred volcano in Korean culture, is located in the DPRK. Traditional naengmyeon (cold buckwheat noodles) and Pyongyang cuisine are recognized food traditions.
MKD: North Macedonia is internationally associated with its connection to Alexander the Great — born in Pella (now in Greece) but descending from the ancient Macedonian kingdom whose territory overlapped with the modern state, making Alexander a subject of significant regional heritage discussions. Lake Ohrid (UNESCO, dual natural and cultural site) is one of Europe's oldest and deepest lakes with exceptional endemic aquatic species and a heritage of early medieval Byzantine and Macedonian Christian churches and manuscripts. The city of Ohrid is internationally recognized for its concentration of Orthodox churches and frescos. Tavče gravče (baked beans in clay pot, the national dish) and rakija are recognized Macedonian food and drink traditions.
MNP: The Northern Mariana Islands is internationally recognized as a US Commonwealth territory in the Western Pacific with significant WWII history — the Battle of Saipan (1944) was one of the war's most significant Pacific engagements. Traditional Chamorro culture (shared with Guam) includes latte stone pillars, chenchule' mutual aid practices, and traditional fiesta foods. The islands' warm-water reefs are internationally recognized diving destinations. The remote island of Farallon de Pajaros (Uracas) is one of the most active volcanoes in the Western Pacific.
OMN: Oman is internationally associated with frankincense — the Dhofar region has been the world's most significant source of high-quality frankincense resin for over 5,000 years, traded via the Incense Route to the ancient Mediterranean, Mesopotamia, and South Asia (UNESCO World Heritage Aflaj irrigation sites and the Land of Frankincense are both listed). Muscat's Mutrah Souk and the fortified coastal city of Nizwa with its traditional silver souk are internationally recognized for traditional Omani silversmithing and khanjar (curved dagger) craftsmanship. The Musandam Peninsula fjords are internationally recognized as 'the Norway of Arabia.' Traditional Omani dhow boat building at Sur is recognized. Shuwa (slow-cooked meat in underground clay pots) and harees are traditional Omani dishes.
PAK: Pakistan is internationally associated with the Indus Valley Civilization — the cities of Mohenjo-daro and Harappa (UNESCO) represent one of the world's four earliest urban civilizations (3300–1300 BCE), with sophisticated drainage systems and standardized weights that predate many other ancient societies. The Karakoram Highway — dubbed the 'Eighth Wonder of the World' — is internationally recognized as one of the world's highest paved international roads, passing through dramatic mountain scenery linking Pakistan and China. Pakistan has the world's second-largest mountain system, with K2 (8,611 m), the world's second-highest peak, and many other 8,000-metre peaks in the Karakoram and Hindukush. Traditional Pakistani truck art — richly decorated commercial vehicles with colourful patterns — is internationally recognized. Biryani, nihari, and chai are widely associated internationally with Pakistani cuisine.
PLW: Palau is internationally associated with its extraordinary marine biodiversity and proactive ocean conservation — the country established the world's first shark sanctuary (2009) and one of the Pacific's largest fully protected marine reserves. Jellyfish Lake on Ongeim'l Tketau island — where visitors swim among millions of non-stinging golden jellyfish — is one of the world's most internationally recognized wildlife swimming experiences. Palau's coral reefs in the Coral Triangle are internationally recognized for their diversity and relative pristine condition. The Rock Islands Southern Lagoon (UNESCO) is both a natural and cultural heritage site. Traditional Palauan bai (meeting houses) with elaborate painted facades are recognized cultural architecture.
PSE: The Palestinian Territories are internationally associated with the ancient heritage of the West Bank and Gaza — Jericho is widely regarded as one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities. Traditional Palestinian embroidery (tatreez, UNESCO Intangible Heritage) is internationally recognized as a textile art form expressing regional and family identity through distinctive cross-stitch patterns. The Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem (UNESCO) marks the traditional birthplace of Jesus Christ and is internationally significant in Christian heritage. Traditional Palestinian food — musakhan (chicken with sumac and onions on taboon bread), maqluba (upside-down rice dish), and knafeh (sweet cheese pastry) — is internationally recognized as part of Levantine cuisine. Palestinian olive cultivation and olive oil production are deeply rooted in the landscape.
PAN: Panama is internationally associated with the Panama Canal — the 80-kilometre waterway connecting the Atlantic and Pacific oceans through the Isthmus of Panama, one of the greatest engineering achievements in history (opened 1914, expanded 2016), through which approximately 3–5% of world trade transits annually. Panama City's contrast between the Old Town (Casco Viejo, UNESCO) and modern skyline is internationally recognized. The indigenous Guna Yala people's mola textile art — hand-stitched reverse appliqué panels — is internationally collected. Panama hats are traditionally woven in Ecuador, not Panama, though the name comes from their international distribution through Panama. Traditional Panamanian cuisine includes sancocho de gallina, arroz con pollo, and tamales.
PNG: Papua New Guinea is internationally associated with its extraordinary cultural diversity — the country has over 800 distinct languages (approximately 12% of the world's languages), the highest linguistic diversity of any country, reflecting thousands of years of isolated cultural development across its mountains, rainforests, and islands. Traditional sing-sing gatherings — where communities in elaborate feathered headdresses, face paint, and traditional dress perform ceremonial dances — are internationally recognized cultural spectacles. The Goroka Show and Mount Hagen Cultural Show are international tourism events. Papua New Guinea's biodiversity includes birds of paradise — 38 of the approximately 42 known species — which are internationally iconic and used in traditional ceremonial dress. Traditional bilum woven bags are a recognized craft.
PRY: Paraguay is internationally associated with the Jesuit Missions of the Guaraní — the UNESCO-listed ruins of mission settlements (La Santísima Trinidad de Paraná, Jesús de Tavarangue) built in the 17th–18th centuries by Jesuit missionaries and Guaraní people reflect a unique social and architectural experiment. Harp music is central to Paraguayan folk musical identity, and polka paraguaya and guarania are recognized national music genres. Guaraní language is co-official alongside Spanish, making Paraguay one of the most bilingual countries in the Americas by actual usage. Tereré — cold yerba mate infusion with cold water or fruit juice — is a nationally beloved drink and holds UNESCO Intangible Heritage status. Sopa paraguaya (a cornmeal cheese bread, despite the name) is the recognized national food.
PHL: The Philippines is internationally associated with whale shark (butanding) encounters — Donsol in Sorsogon province is recognized as one of the world's premier sites for swimming alongside the world's largest fish in the wild. Tubbataha Reef Natural Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in the Sulu Sea, is internationally ranked among the world's best dive destinations for its pristine coral atolls and extraordinary marine biodiversity. The Batad and Banaue Ifugao Rice Terraces — 2,000-year-old UNESCO World Heritage terraced rice fields carved into the Cordillera mountains — are globally recognized as an engineering marvel of indigenous agriculture. Jeepneys — brightly decorated public minibuses converted from US military vehicles and customized with colourful murals and chrome ornaments — are an internationally recognized symbol of Filipino creative culture. Filipino bayanihan (communal cooperation) and the adobo dish (meat braised in vinegar and soy sauce) are internationally known cultural exports. The Chocolate Hills of Bohol and Boracay's white-sand beaches are globally recognized natural landmarks. The Philippines is a significant remittance economy through its internationally mobile workforce of nurses, seafarers, and engineers.
PCN: Pitcairn Island is internationally recognized as one of the world's most remote and smallest inhabited territories — a British Overseas Territory with a permanent population of less than 100, all descendants of the HMS Bounty mutineers (1789) and their Tahitian companions. The ship's wreck, still visible underwater at Bounty Bay, is internationally known from the multiple film adaptations of the Mutiny on the Bounty story. Pitcairn islanders produce distinctive hand-carved wooden souvenirs and honey for sale through passing ships. The island is accessible only by boat.
PRI: Puerto Rico is internationally associated with reggaetón — the genre that emerged in San Juan in the 1990s and became one of the world's most-streamed music genres globally, with artists such as Daddy Yankee, Bad Bunny, and J Balvin (of Colombian heritage) bringing the genre to international audiences. Old San Juan's fortress walls — El Morro and San Cristóbal (UNESCO) — are internationally recognized Spanish colonial military architecture. Traditional Puerto Rican cuisine includes mofongo (mashed fried plantains), pernil (slow-roasted pork), arroz con gandules, and tres leches cake. The Arecibo Observatory (prior to 2020) was internationally recognized in radio astronomy and was featured in popular science and film. Puerto Rican salsa and bomba music are internationally recognized.
QAT: Qatar is internationally associated with hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup — the first Middle Eastern country to host the tournament and the first to use air-conditioned stadiums built for the competition. Al Jazeera Media Network, headquartered in Doha, is internationally recognized as a major global Arabic-language news broadcaster. The Museum of Islamic Art in Doha (designed by I.M. Pei) is internationally recognized in contemporary museum architecture. Qatar is one of the world's largest exporters of liquefied natural gas (LNG). Traditional Qatari pearl diving heritage and dhow boat racing culture are recognized. Camel racing, with jockey robots replacing traditional riders, is an internationally discussed sporting tradition. Majlis hospitality culture and dallah (coffee pot) symbolism are traditional expressions.
ROU: Romania is internationally associated with Transylvania and the Dracula legend — Bram Stoker's 1897 novel, inspired partly by the historical figure Vlad III ('the Impaler'), established a global association between Transylvania's medieval castles (particularly Bran Castle) and vampire mythology, driving significant international tourism. Traditional Romanian painted monasteries of Bucovina (UNESCO) — with exterior Byzantine frescoes from the 15th–16th centuries — are internationally recognized as outstanding religious art. The Danube Delta (UNESCO) is one of Europe's largest and best-preserved wetland biodiversity reserves. Traditional Romanian folk music, wood-carving, and carpet-weaving traditions are recognized. Mămăligă (cornmeal porridge), ciorba (sour soup), and mici (grilled sausages) are traditional Romanian foods. Romanian gymnasts have historically achieved outstanding international results.
RWA: Rwanda is internationally associated with mountain gorilla conservation — the Volcanoes National Park, where the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund operates and where the film Gorillas in the Mist (1988) was set, is a globally significant gorilla trekking destination and conservation success story. Rwanda's post-genocide reconciliation and rapid development have been internationally cited as a governance transformation model. Traditional Rwandan intore dance (UNESCO) — a ceremonial warrior dance with elaborate costumes — is a recognized cultural performance tradition. Kigali is internationally recognized as one of Africa's cleanest and best-governed capitals. Traditional Rwandan basketry (agaseke) weaving is internationally collected. Rwanda Cup coffee is internationally recognized in specialty coffee markets.
REU: Réunion is internationally recognized for its extraordinary volcanic landscape — the island contains Piton de la Fournaise, one of the world's most active volcanoes, and the Piton des Neiges (the highest peak in the Indian Ocean islands). The cirques (steep-sided natural amphitheatres of Cilaos, Mafate, and Salazie) are internationally recognized for trekking. The island's Piton de la Fournaise, the cirques, and the ramparts together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Réunion's Creole culture blends African, Indian, French, and Chinese traditions in music, food, and language. Traditional séga and maloya music (UNESCO) are recognized cultural expressions. Rougail saucisse (sausage curry) and cari poulet (chicken curry) are traditional dishes.
BLM: Saint Barthélemy (Saint-Barths) is internationally recognized as an exclusive luxury French Caribbean destination favoured by international celebrities and high-net-worth tourists, associated with quiet beaches (Saline, Gouverneur), high-end boutiques in Gustavia, and upscale villas. The island has Swedish colonial heritage (Swedish rule 1784–1878), visible in its place names and the Swedish flag incorporated in its seal. Gustavia port hosts luxury yachts during the international sailing season. The island is a French overseas collectivity.
SHN: Saint Helena is internationally recognized as the remote South Atlantic island where Napoleon Bonaparte was exiled from 1815 until his death in 1821 — his residence at Longwood House and tomb (prior to repatriation to Paris in 1840) are internationally referenced sites in Napoleonic history. The island's extremely isolated position made it a strategic resupply point for ships rounding Africa before the Suez Canal opened. Jonathan, a Seychellois giant tortoise believed to be born around 1832, is one of the world's oldest known living land animals and has become internationally recognized. The island is a British Overseas Territory. Direct flights to Saint Helena Airport (opened 2016) ended centuries of ship-only access.
KNA: Saint Kitts and Nevis is internationally associated with Brimstone Hill Fortress (UNESCO) — a British colonial fortification commanding the island's most defensible position, constructed by enslaved African labour over a century and known as 'the Gibraltar of the West Indies.' The federation is the smallest sovereign state in the Western Hemisphere by land area. Traditional steelpan music (shared with broader Caribbean tradition) and masquerade dance performances are cultural expressions. Christopher Columbus named the island for Saint Christopher (his patron saint) in 1493. Nevis, the sister island, was the birthplace of Alexander Hamilton, the American Founding Father.
LCA: Saint Lucia is internationally associated with the Pitons (UNESCO) — Gros Piton and Petit Piton, two distinctive volcanic spires rising steeply from the Caribbean Sea near Soufrière, are internationally recognized as among the most striking natural landmarks in the Caribbean. The island is recognized as the birthplace of two Nobel Prize winners (Derek Walcott, Literature, 1992; Arthur Lewis, Economics, 1979), which is notable for a small island nation. Castries Saturday morning market is known for local spices, cocoa, and tropical produce. Traditional Saint Lucian Creole cuisine includes green fig and saltfish, breadfruit, and bouillon. The island's carnival, jazz festival, and traditional La Rose and La Marguerite folk societies are cultural traditions.
MAF: Saint Martin (French side) shares the island of Sint Maarten with the Netherlands Antilles in a unique jurisdictional arrangement — the island is divided between France and the Netherlands in an agreement dating to 1648. The French side, Saint-Martin, is a French collectivity internationally known for its beaches, particularly Orient Beach, and duty-free shopping in Marigot. The island is internationally noted for being the smallest territory in the world to be divided between two sovereign states.
SPM: Saint Pierre and Miquelon is internationally noted as the only remaining French territory in North America — two small islands off the southern coast of Newfoundland, Canada, reflecting France's former colonial empire in the region. The islands have a distinctly French fishing village culture and architecture. During Prohibition (1920–1933), the islands were reportedly used as a whisky transshipment point for smuggling to the United States. Traditional cod fishing was the historical economic foundation.
VCT: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is internationally associated with the filming of the Pirates of the Caribbean franchise (2003–2007) on location among the Grenadine islands — the distinctive landscape of volcanic St. Vincent and the palm-fringed beaches of the Grenadines (Bequia, Mustique, Tobago Cays) are internationally recognized as Caribbean sailing and yacht charter destinations. Mustique island is internationally known as a private island resort associated with celebrity and royal visitors. Traditional Saint Vincentian breadfruit, arrowroot production, and roasted breadfruit are associated with the island's culinary heritage. The Soufrière volcano is historically active.
WSM: Samoa is internationally associated with the fa'a Samoa ('the Samoan Way') — a cultural value system emphasizing communal family (aiga) obligations, respect for elders (matai chiefly system), and shared responsibility that is practiced by Samoan communities worldwide. Traditional siapo (tapa cloth) made from beaten mulberry bark with geometric patterns, and fine mats (ie toga) woven from pandanus, are internationally recognized Samoan prestige craft traditions. Samoan tattoo (pe'a for men, malu for women) — distinctive curvilinear geometric tattoos applied with traditional combs by a tufuga tā tatau specialist — are internationally recognized among the world's oldest living tattoo traditions. Robert Louis Stevenson spent his final years in Samoa and is buried there.
SMR: San Marino is internationally recognized as the world's oldest republic (founded, by tradition, in 301 CE) and one of the world's smallest countries, an enclaved microstate within Italy. The Three Towers of San Marino — Guaita, Cesta, and Montale — are internationally recognized medieval fortifications on the rocky peak of Monte Titano (UNESCO World Heritage Site). San Marino has no army and no income tax. The country has notable postage stamp and coin collecting communities internationally due to its separate production of philatelic and numismatic items. Traditional Sammarinese cuisine is similar to Emilian-Romagnol Italian cooking, with piadina flatbread, passatelli pasta, and local white wine.
SAU: Saudi Arabia is internationally associated with Islam's two holiest cities — Mecca and Medina — which together attract approximately 2 million Muslim pilgrims during the annual Hajj pilgrimage, making the Hajj the world's largest annual religious gathering. Saudi Arabia is the world's largest oil exporter and home to Ghawar Field, the world's largest conventional oil field.
