The ancient Nabataean city of Hegra (AlUla, UNESCO) — rock-carved tombs similar to Petra — is internationally recognized. Traditional Saudi Arabian coffee (Arabic coffee, qahwa) served in small cups with dates is a recognized hospitality ritual. Camel racing, falconry (UNESCO), and traditional sword dance (Ardah, UNESCO) are recognized cultural traditions. The futuristic megacity project NEOM represents an internationally discussed urban development concept.
SEN: Senegal is internationally associated with Teranga — the Wolof concept of hospitality and generosity — internationally recognized as embodying the country's welcoming culture. The music of Senegal, particularly mbalax (internationally popularized by Youssou N'Dour) with its sabar drum polyrhythms, is a significant African musical contribution. The island of Gorée (UNESCO) — a former slave trading post off Dakar — is internationally significant in African diaspora heritage. Wrestling (laamb) is Senegal's most popular spectator sport and a major cultural event. Dakar Rally (now held in South America) took its name from Senegal. Traditional Senegalese cuisine includes thiéboudienne (fish and rice, UNESCO), Yassa poulet (chicken with caramelized onions and citrus), and attaya (mint tea ceremony).
SRB: Serbia is internationally associated with Nikola Tesla — the inventor and electrical engineer who developed alternating current (AC) electrical systems and the rotating magnetic field was born in Smiljan (now Croatia) to Serbian parents and is a source of national pride in Serbia. Traditional Serbian rakija (fruit brandy, particularly šljivovica plum brandy, UNESCO) is internationally recognized. The EXIT Music Festival in Novi Sad has gained international recognition as one of Europe's best music festivals. Serbian tennis players, particularly Novak Djokovic, have achieved unprecedented international success. Sobranje (parliament) architecture in Belgrade and the Kalemegdan fortress are heritage landmarks. Traditional Serbian cuisine includes ćevapi, pljeskavica, and sarma (stuffed cabbage).
SYC: Seychelles is internationally associated with its inner island granite formations — the islands of Mahé, Praslin, and La Digue feature distinctive prehistoric granite boulders (among the world's oldest ocean granite) and palm-fringed white-sand beaches that have become internationally iconic images of remote island paradise. The coco de mer palm — producing the world's largest seed (up to 25 kilograms) — is endemic to Praslin and is internationally recognized as a botanical curiosity. The Vallée de Mai on Praslin (UNESCO) is an ancient palm forest internationally recognized for its primeval atmosphere. Aldabra Atoll (UNESCO), an elevated coral atoll with the world's second-largest Aldabra giant tortoise population, is internationally significant in conservation. Seychellois Creole cuisine features coconut-infused fish curries.
SLE: Sierra Leone is internationally associated with the diamond trade — alluvial diamond deposits in the Kono district and the historical significance of conflict diamonds ('blood diamonds') in funding civil war became internationally recognized through the 2006 Leonardo DiCaprio film Blood Diamond. The country's recovery and reconciliation process has been internationally studied as a post-conflict development case. Bunce Island in the Sierra Leone River was a significant British slave trading post, connecting the country to African American and Gullah Geechee heritage in the American South (many rice farmers from Sierra Leone were transported to the Carolinas). Traditional Mende and Temne mask traditions are internationally recognized African art forms. Rice is the dietary and cultural staple.
SXM: Sint Maarten (Dutch side) shares the island of Saint Martin with France in a unique administrative arrangement. The Dutch side is internationally recognized for Princess Juliana International Airport, where arriving aircraft pass extremely low over Maho Beach — creating a world-famous aviation photography and tourism spectacle. The island is a significant cruise ship port. Traditional Dutch Caribbean architecture and duty-free shopping are tourism features.
SVK: Slovakia is internationally associated with its exceptional medieval castle heritage — the country has approximately 180 castles and castle ruins per square kilometre, including Spiš Castle (UNESCO), one of the largest castle complexes in Central Europe. The Banská Štiavnica mining town (UNESCO) and Vlkolínec village (UNESCO) represent outstanding examples of Central European heritage. Traditional Slovak folk music and dance — including fujara (a bass shepherd's flute, UNESCO) — are internationally recognized. Slovak spa culture, particularly in Piešťany, is a recognized wellness tradition. Slovak cuisine includes bryndzové halušky (potato dumplings with sheep cheese, recognized as the national dish) and kapustnica (sauerkraut soup).
SVN: Slovenia is internationally recognized for Škocjan Caves (UNESCO) — a vast underground canyon with chambers up to 100 metres high and the Reka River creating extraordinary speleothem formations, considered among the world's most significant karst cave systems. Predjama Castle — a Renaissance castle built into a cave mouth in a cliffside — is internationally recognized as an architectural curiosity. Lake Bled with its island church and clifftop castle is one of the most internationally recognized alpine lake landscapes in Europe. Traditional Slovenian cuisine includes potica (nut roll pastry, UNESCO), kranjska klobasa (Carniolan sausage), and idrijski žlikrofi (filled pasta, UNESCO). Slovenia is recognized for its hop production used in beer brewing.
SLB: The Solomon Islands is internationally recognized for the naval Battle of Guadalcanal (1942–43) — one of the most significant and costly engagements of the Pacific War, in which the United States and Japan fought for control of Guadalcanal island in a campaign lasting approximately six months. Iron Bottom Sound (named for the large number of sunken ships) is internationally known among WWII historians and divers. The Solomon Islands' reefs and lagoons feature exceptional marine biodiversity. Traditional kastom culture includes intricate shell money traditions, carved wooden toto'o trolling hooks, and unique bonito cult ceremonies. The Vitu Islands and Marovo Lagoon (UNESCO Tentative) feature significant coral reef ecosystems.
SOM: Somalia is internationally associated with Mogadishu and its ancient Indian Ocean trade heritage — Somali city-states were major trading hubs for the East African coast, exporting frankincense, myrrh, gold, and ivory to Arabia, Persia, and India. The Somali camel herding tradition is central to pastoralist culture and economy, with Somalia having one of the world's largest camel populations. Xeer — Somalia's traditional customary law system — is internationally studied as an example of stateless legal practice. Somali poetry is a richly developed oral tradition internationally recognized in comparative literature. Sambusa (fried pastry), canjeero (spongy bread), and suqaar (spiced meat) are traditional Somali foods. Somali bananas were historically exported from the Shebelle River valley.
SGS: South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands is internationally recognized as the site of the largest colony of king penguins in the world — the beaches of South Georgia, particularly at St. Andrews Bay and Salisbury Plain, host colonies of hundreds of thousands of king penguins and are internationally recognized in wildlife photography and documentary media. The island is the burial site of Antarctic explorer Ernest Shackleton (1874–1922). South Georgia's sub-Antarctic ecosystem supports elephant seals, fur seals, and enormous seabird populations. The territory is uninhabited except for research station staff.
SSD: South Sudan is internationally recognized for the Sudd — one of the world's largest tropical freshwater wetland ecosystems, formed by the White Nile's seasonal flooding of the South Sudanese plains, supporting diverse wildlife and migratory birds. The country became the world's newest recognized nation upon independence from Sudan (2011). The Mundari people's cattle herding traditions and distinctive Nilotic cultural practices (including cattle camp life and scarification traditions) have been internationally documented. The Dinka people's rich oral poetry, cattle-wealth culture, and traditional jumping dance are internationally noted cultural practices.
LKA: Sri Lanka is internationally associated with Ceylon tea — the country was historically the world's largest tea exporter, and 'Ceylon tea' remains an internationally recognized premium product designation despite the country's name change in 1972. Sigiriya (Lion Rock, UNESCO) — a 5th-century royal citadel built on a 200-metre granite rock, with frescoes and elaborate water gardens — is internationally recognized as an extraordinary archaeological site. The Tooth Relic of the Buddha (Dalada Maligawa temple in Kandy, UNESCO) is among Buddhism's most sacred relics. Traditional Kandyan dance (UNESCO) and Kolam mask performance are recognized art forms. Sri Lankan cuisine — including rice and curry, kottu roti, hoppers (appe), and pol sambol — is internationally recognized for its aromatic spice complexity.
SDN: Sudan is internationally associated with the ancient Nubian kingdom of Kush and Meroe — the Nubian pyramids at Meroe (UNESCO), slightly smaller but more numerous than Egyptian pyramids, represent an internationally significant African pyramid tradition, built by the Kingdom of Kush between approximately 700 BCE and 350 CE. Sudan has more ancient pyramid structures than Egypt. The ancient Kerma and Nuri archaeological sites reflect significant Nubian civilization. The Nile River — and the confluence of the Blue Nile and White Nile near Khartoum — is geographically and historically significant. Traditional Nubian music and culture are distinct from Arab Sudanese traditions. Ful medames (fava bean stew) and kisra (sorghum flatbread) are traditional foods.
SUR: Suriname is internationally associated with its position as a former Dutch colony with the smallest population of any sovereign state in South America — and notably as the only Dutch-speaking nation outside Europe and the Kingdom of the Netherlands proper (in South America). Paramaribo's historic inner city (UNESCO) features Dutch colonial plantation-era wooden architecture built in tropical conditions, alongside mosques and synagogues reflecting the country's multicultural heritage. Suriname's interior Amazon basin contains indigenous Amerindian and Maroon communities (descendants of escaped enslaved people who established independent forest communities) with distinct cultural traditions. Traditional Surinamese cuisine reflects multi-ethnic heritage including roti, bara, and pom (layered casserole).
SJM: Svalbard and Jan Mayen is internationally recognized for the Svalbard Archipelago's dramatic Arctic landscape and globally significant polar bear population — with more polar bears than human residents, Svalbard is internationally associated with Arctic wildlife encounters and research. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault (established 2008) — carved into permafrost in a mountain near Longyearbyen — is an internationally recognized effort to safeguard agricultural biodiversity, housing seeds from virtually all known plant species used in agriculture. Svalbard is governed under the Svalbard Treaty, which gives all treaty signatories equal rights to exploit resources. The Midnight Sun and polar night are dramatic seasonal phenomena.
SYR: Syria is internationally associated with Damascus — one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, with a history of over 10,000 years, whose ancient city (UNESCO) includes the Great Mosque of the Umayyads (8th century), one of Islam's oldest and most significant mosques. Aleppo's Old City (UNESCO) and the ancient Silk Road trade history made Syria a centre of international commerce and intellectual exchange. Traditional Syrian cuisine — kibbeh, shawarma, baklava, fatteh, and Aleppo pepper — is internationally recognized as part of Levantine gastronomy. Syrian craft traditions, particularly Damascene inlay work (intarsia), silk brocade (damask fabric takes its name from Damascus), and blown glass are internationally recognized.
STP: São Tomé and Príncipe is internationally associated with premium cacao production — the small island nation in the Gulf of Guinea produces internationally recognized fine-flavour cocoa beans used by premium chocolate makers, particularly from the Claudio Corallo and other single-origin producers. The Portuguese colonial plantation (roça) system, with distinctive colonial architecture converted to hotels and farms, is an internationally noted cultural heritage. São Tomé's endemic bird species — including the São Tomé fiscal and São Tomé giant sunbird — are internationally recognized in ornithology. The islands' equatorial rainforest and dramatic volcanic landscape attract ecotourism. Calulu (fish or meat stew with tropical leaves) is a traditional dish.
TJK: Tajikistan is internationally associated with the Pamir Mountains — known as 'the Roof of the World,' the Pamirs contain some of the world's highest altitude valleys and peaks (including Ismoil Somoni Peak at 7,495 metres), with traditional Pamiri culture expressed in distinctive wooden house architecture, woven carpet patterns, and oral poetry. The ancient Silk Road passed through Tajik territory, with Samarkand-related trade routes connecting Central Asia to China and Persia. Traditional Tajik music using the dutar lute and rubab instrument are regionally recognized. Tajik cuisine includes plov (rice and meat pilaf), samsa, and naan. The Tajik National Epic (Shahnameh traditions, shared with Persian literary heritage) is culturally central.
TZA: Tanzania is internationally associated with Serengeti National Park (UNESCO) and the Great Wildebeest Migration — the annual circular migration of approximately 1.5 million wildebeest, 400,000 zebra, and 200,000 gazelles across the Serengeti-Masai Mara ecosystem is internationally recognized as one of the world's greatest wildlife spectacles. Mount Kilimanjaro, the highest peak in Africa (5,895 metres), is internationally recognized for accessible high-altitude trekking to its snow-capped summit above the equatorial plain. Zanzibar's Stone Town (UNESCO) reflects Arab, Indian, Persian, and East African trading heritage. Tanzania is home to the Olduvai Gorge — where early human ancestor fossils have been discovered — and the Ngorongoro Crater (UNESCO). Traditional Tanzanian cuisine includes ugali with nyama choma, pilau rice, and coconut-based Swahili dishes.
TLS: Timor-Leste (East Timor) is internationally recognized as one of the world's youngest nations, having achieved independence from Indonesia in 2002 after a long independence struggle. The country's sacred tais woven cloth — a textile tradition with distinct regional patterns — is internationally recognized as a cultural expression. The Atauro Island marine environment and Timor Sea reefs are internationally recognized for marine biodiversity and dive tourism. Traditional Timorese music includes likurai drum performance by women. Timor-Leste's coffee — particularly from the Ermera and Aileu regions — is internationally traded in specialty markets as a fine, distinctive single-origin coffee. The José Ramos-Horta and Xanana Gusmão-led independence narrative is internationally recognized in human rights history.
TGO: Togo is internationally associated with its traditional voodoo (Vodun) practices — the Akodessawa Fetish Market in Lomé is internationally recognized as the world's largest voodoo market, selling traditional spiritual objects, animal parts, and ritual items. Togo's cultural heritage reflects the meeting of Fon, Ewe, and other West African peoples. Traditional Ewe kente weaving (shared with Ghanaian Ewe tradition) produces distinct geometric textile patterns. Togoland was the site of the first German colonial surrender in WWI. Traditional Togolese cuisine includes fufu with palm nut soup, akoumé (corn porridge), and grilled brochettes.
TKL: Tokelau is internationally recognized as one of the world's most isolated and least-visited territories — three coral atolls in the Pacific Ocean with a total population of approximately 1,500, accessible only by a two-day boat journey from Samoa. Tokelau was the first territory in the world to derive 100% of its electricity from solar power. The Tokelauan inati communal sharing system — distributing fish and resources equally across the community — is an internationally noted example of communal resource governance. Tokelau is a New Zealand non-self-governing territory.
TON: Tonga is internationally recognized as the world's last remaining Polynesian monarchy — the Kingdom of Tonga maintained its sovereign independence throughout the colonial era, a distinction unique among Pacific Island nations. Traditional Tongan ngatu (bark cloth) and fine mat (kie) weaving are recognized ceremonial craft traditions. Humpback whale calving and mating occurs in Tongan waters each year (July–October), and swimming with humpback whales in Tonga is internationally recognized as a distinctive wildlife experience. Traditional Tongan feast preparation (umu earth oven) and kava ceremonies are culturally significant. Tongan rugby union players have made significant contributions to international rugby, particularly in Super Rugby and international tournaments.
TTO: Trinidad and Tobago is internationally associated with the invention of the steel pan (steelpan) — the only acoustic musical instrument developed in the 20th century, born in Port of Spain when musicians discovered that petrol oil drum lids could produce musical pitches, the instrument has spread globally and is internationally recognized as Trinidad's cultural gift to the world. The Trinidad Carnival — with its competitive soca music, calypso artistry, and elaborate mas band costume processions — is internationally recognized as one of the world's great carnival celebrations. Trinidad is also the birthplace of calypso and chutney soca music traditions. The Pitch Lake in La Brea, a naturally occurring asphalt lake, is internationally recognized as a geological curiosity. Doubles (curried chickpea on bara flatbread) is a recognized Trinidadian street food internationally.
TUN: Tunisia is internationally associated with the ancient city of Carthage (UNESCO) — founded in the 9th century BCE by Phoenician settlers, Carthage became one of the ancient world's great powers and rival of Rome before its destruction in 146 BCE, leaving internationally significant archaeological ruins near Tunis. The Medina of Tunis (UNESCO) features outstanding Arab-Islamic architecture. Tunisia's tourism is internationally associated with the Sahara Desert landscape — the salt flats and dunes of Douz and the Chott el-Djerid provided the filming locations for Tatooine in the Star Wars franchise. Traditional Tunisian cuisine includes harissa chilli paste, brik (egg pastry), couscous, and mechouia salad. The Carthage film festival is internationally recognized in African and Arab cinema.
TKM: Turkmenistan is internationally associated with the Darvaza gas crater — dubbed the 'Door to Hell' or 'Gates of Hell,' a natural gas field that collapsed into an underground cavern and has been burning continuously since approximately 1971, creating an internationally recognized flaming crater spectacle in the Karakum Desert. Traditional Turkmen carpet weaving is internationally recognized — the Turkmen carpet (hali) is a UNESCO Intangible Heritage and the carpet motif (gul) appears on the national flag, with Turkmenistan being among the world's most famous carpet-producing nations. The ancient Silk Road city of Merv (UNESCO) was historically one of the world's largest cities and an important centre of Islamic scholarship. Traditional akhal-teke horse breed, internationally recognized for its metallic coat sheen, originates in Turkmenistan.
TCA: The Turks and Caicos Islands is internationally recognized as an ultra-clear Caribbean water destination — Grace Bay Beach on Providenciales is consistently rated among the world's most beautiful beaches for its powdery sand and transparent shallow water. The territory is internationally associated with conch — large queen conch shells and conch fritters are traditional elements of the local culture and culinary tradition. The Turks and Caicos is a British Overseas Territory and a significant offshore financial services jurisdiction. The annual Caicos Conch Festival celebrates the island's conch heritage.
TUV: Tuvalu is internationally recognized as one of the countries most existentially threatened by climate change and sea-level rise — as one of the world's lowest-lying nations (highest point approximately 4.5 metres), Tuvalu has been at the forefront of international discussions on climate justice and Pacific Island vulnerability. The country has the world's second-smallest population of any sovereign state. Tuvalu's '.tv' internet domain suffix has been significantly commercially valuable and is used by television broadcasters worldwide, providing a significant source of revenue. Traditional fatele dance performances and communal maneapa (meeting house) governance are cultural practices.
UGA: Uganda is internationally associated with mountain gorilla conservation in Bwindi Impenetrable Forest (UNESCO) — together with Rwanda and the DRC, Uganda protects more than half of the world's remaining mountain gorilla population. The source of the Nile River — flowing northward from Lake Victoria at Jinja — is internationally recognized as a geographic landmark. The Buganda Kingdom's royal heritage, including Kasubi Tombs (UNESCO), is a significant East African heritage site. Traditional Ugandan music includes amadinda xylophone (UNESCO) and endongo bow-harp traditions. Matooke (steamed plantain), rolex (egg omelette in chapati), and groundnut stew are widely recognized Ugandan foods. Uganda's Pearl of Africa designation refers to its extraordinary biodiversity and landscape.
UKR: Ukraine is internationally associated with its sunflower fields — vast golden sunflower plantations across the Black Sea steppe have made Ukraine the world's leading producer and exporter of sunflower oil, and the sunflower has become internationally symbolic of Ukraine. Pysanky — elaborately decorated Easter eggs using wax-resist dyeing with intricate geometric and symbolic patterns — are internationally recognized as a Ukrainian craft tradition. The city of Kyiv's Pechersk Lavra (Monastery of the Caves, UNESCO) and St. Sophia's Cathedral (UNESCO) are significant Orthodox Christian heritage sites. Traditional Ukrainian embroidery (vyshyvanka shirt) is internationally recognized in folk textile traditions. Ukrainian borscht (beet soup, UNESCO), varenyky (dumplings), and holubtsi (stuffed cabbage) are internationally recognized foods.
ARE: The United Arab Emirates is internationally associated with Dubai's futuristic skyline — the Burj Khalifa (the world's tallest building at 828 metres), Palm Jumeirah (an artificial palm-shaped island), and other bold architectural projects have made Dubai one of the world's most internationally recognized cityscapes of the 21st century. Abu Dhabi's Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque is internationally recognized as one of the world's largest mosques and a significant example of contemporary Islamic architecture. Traditional Emirati falconry (UNESCO) and camel racing are recognized heritage practices. The Dubai World Expo (2020/21) attracted global participation. Traditional Arabic coffee (qahwa) with dates hospitality, and the abaya and kandura traditional dress are associated with Emirati culture.
UMI: The United States Minor Outlying Islands are a collection of US territories in the Pacific Ocean and Caribbean — including Wake Island, Midway Atoll, Johnston Atoll, and Palmyra Atoll — with no permanent civilian population. Wake Island was a significant Pacific War site (Japanese capture of the island in December 1941 followed Pearl Harbor). Midway Atoll is internationally recognized for the Battle of Midway (1942), a pivotal naval air battle, and for its black-footed albatross colony (the world's largest Laysan albatross nesting colony). The territories are primarily used for US military and scientific purposes.
VIR: The United States Virgin Islands is internationally recognized for its history as a former Danish colony (Danish West Indies, purchased by the United States in 1917) — this heritage is reflected in the gingerbread architectural style of Christiansted (UNESCO), which blends Danish colonial and Caribbean elements. Charlotte Amalie, the capital, was a historically significant free port in the Caribbean. The Virgin Islands Carnival, carnival jouvert, and traditional quelbe music (considered the official music of the USVI) are recognized cultural traditions. The Buck Island Reef National Monument and underwater snorkeling trail are federally protected marine sites. Traditional local foods include saltfish and dumplings, mauby (bark drink), and coconut tart.
URY: Uruguay is internationally associated with tango — though the music and dance form is most internationally associated with Argentina, Uruguay (particularly Montevideo) claims a parallel origin and has its own distinct tango tradition. Uruguay was the first country in the world to legalize and regulate the sale of marijuana (2013), an internationally cited drug policy reform. The historic Colonia del Sacramento (UNESCO) — a Portuguese colonial trading town on the Río de la Plata — features exceptional cobblestone streets and colonial architecture. Traditional Uruguayan asado (barbecue culture, among the highest per-capita beef consumption in the world) and chivito (steak sandwich) are internationally recognized food traditions. Candombe (UNESCO), an Afro-Uruguayan drumming tradition, is recognized in world music contexts.
UZB: Uzbekistan is internationally associated with the ancient Silk Road cities of Samarkand, Bukhara, and Khiva — the turquoise-tiled domes of the Registan square in Samarkand (UNESCO), the Kalon Minaret of Bukhara (UNESCO), and the walled Ichan-Kala of Khiva (UNESCO) represent outstanding examples of Timurid and Central Asian Islamic architecture, internationally recognized for their brilliant tile work. The Timurid dynasty under Timur (Tamerlane) and his successor Ulugh Beg patronized a golden age of Persian-influenced architecture and science. Traditional Uzbek crafts — suzani embroidery, Ikat silk weaving, and wood carving — are internationally collected. Traditional Uzbek plov (rice pilaf cooked in a large kazan, UNESCO) is internationally recognized as the culinary centrepiece of Uzbek culture.
VUT: Vanuatu is internationally associated with land diving (naghol) on Pentecost Island — the traditional ritual in which men tie liana vines to their ankles and leap from tall wooden towers to ensure a good yam harvest is internationally recognized as the world's original bungee jumping predecessor and one of the Pacific's most dramatic rituals. Vanuatu has the world's most linguistically diverse population relative to its size, with approximately 130 languages spoken by around 300,000 people. The Yasur volcano on Tanna island — one of the world's most accessible active volcanoes — allows visitors to approach the active lava lake. Chief Roy Mata's Domain (UNESCO) is a recognized Vanuatu heritage site.
VAT: Vatican City is internationally recognized as the world's smallest sovereign state by both area and population, and the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church — the spiritual home for approximately 1.4 billion Catholics worldwide. St. Peter's Basilica and the Vatican Museums (including the Sistine Chapel with Michelangelo's ceiling fresco) are among the most internationally visited cultural and religious sites in the world, attracting millions of visitors annually. The Vatican is the world's only state whose primary official language is Latin. The Papal conclave (the process of electing a new Pope, with white smoke signalling a successful vote) is an internationally followed media event. The Vatican Archives and Library contain historically significant documents.
VEN: Venezuela is internationally associated with Angel Falls (Salto Ángel) — the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall, plunging approximately 979 metres from Auyán-tepui table mountain in Canaima National Park (UNESCO), it is one of South America's most internationally recognized natural landmarks. The tepui (table-top mountain) landscape of the Gran Sabana — flat-topped mesas rising dramatically from the savanna — is internationally recognized in both geography and as the setting for Arthur Conan Doyle's novel The Lost World. Venezuela has the world's largest proven oil reserves. Traditional Venezuelan music includes joropo (UNESCO) played on cuatro (four-string guitar) and arpa llanera (harp). Hallacas (cornmeal parcels stuffed with stew, wrapped in banana leaves) are the recognized national Christmas dish.
WLF: Wallis and Futuna is a French collectivity in the South Pacific — a group of three main volcanic islands between Samoa and Fiji with a combined population of approximately 11,000. The territory has a unique political structure respecting three traditional kingdoms (Uvea, Sigave, and Alo) operating alongside French administrative authority. Traditional Polynesian cultural practices, including kava ceremonies and traditional tapa cloth, are maintained. The islands have no public transport system and limited road infrastructure.
ESH: Western Sahara is internationally associated with the Saharan Desert landscape and the contested political status between Morocco and the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (POLISARIO Front) — one of Africa's last unresolved decolonization disputes, internationally referenced in UN discussions since 1975. The region's Atlantic coast fisheries are among the world's most productive. The Sahrawi people maintain a distinct Hassaniya Arabic cultural identity expressed in traditional tent living, camel herding, and distinctive blue robes (daraa). Traditional Sahrawi music featuring the tbal drum and tidinit lute is culturally significant.
YEM: Yemen is internationally associated with the ancient incense trade — Yemen (historical Arabia Felix) was the source or transit point for frankincense and myrrh in the ancient world, and the incense route from Yemen to the Mediterranean was among antiquity's most economically significant trading corridors. The Old City of Sana'a (UNESCO) features extraordinary multi-storey mud-brick tower houses decorated with white gypsum plasterwork in a distinctive architectural tradition. The Socotra Archipelago (UNESCO) is internationally recognized for its surreal endemic vegetation — the dragon blood tree (Dracaena cinnabari) with its umbrella-shaped canopy is internationally distinctive and found nowhere else. Traditional Yemeni coffee culture — qishr (coffee husk ginger drink) and origins of the Mocha coffee bean — is internationally significant in coffee history. Bint al-sahn (honey cake) and saltah (national stew) are recognized Yemeni foods.
ZMB: Zambia is internationally recognized for Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya, UNESCO) — shared with Zimbabwe, the world's largest waterfall by combined width and height creates a spray visible from 20 kilometres away, and the Zambezi River crossing the falls in flood season is internationally recognized as one of the world's great natural spectacles. The Devil's Pool — a natural infinity-pool rock depression at the lip of Victoria Falls — is an internationally noted extreme tourism experience. South Luangwa National Park is internationally recognized in wildlife safari circles for its walking safari tradition. Traditional Zambian cuisine includes nshima (maize porridge) with relishes of dried fish, beans, and greens. The copper-belt region historically made Zambia one of the world's major copper producers.
ZWE: Zimbabwe is internationally associated with Great Zimbabwe (UNESCO) — the ancient stone-walled city complex whose ruins represent the largest stone structure in sub-Saharan Africa south of the Sahara, built without mortar between the 11th and 15th centuries and demonstrating advanced pre-colonial African urban civilization. The country's name is derived from this site. Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya, UNESCO, shared with Zambia) is internationally recognized as one of Africa's most spectacular natural landmarks. Traditional Shona stone sculpture — Zimbabwe's internationally recognized contemporary art form, particularly large-scale abstract soapstone works — has been internationally exhibited and collected since the 1950s. Traditional mbira music (thumb piano, UNESCO) is a recognized Zimbabwean musical heritage.
ALA: Åland Islands is an autonomous, demilitarized, Swedish-speaking archipelago of approximately 6,700 islands belonging to Finland but with its own parliament, flag, postal stamps, and licence plates. The islands are internationally recognized for their maritime heritage — Mariehamn was the home port of the last major commercial sailing ship fleet in the world (Erikson Line, active until the 1950s), and the Åland Maritime Museum displays this tradition. The Åland Peace Agreement (1921) established the demilitarization and autonomy that makes the islands internationally noted in international law. Åland's apple orchards and elk hunting are associated with the local culture. The islands attract Scandinavian sailing and summer holiday visitors.
CIV: Côte d'Ivoire (Ivory Coast) is internationally associated with cocoa production — the country is the world's largest producer and exporter of cocoa beans, supplying approximately 40% of global cocoa output and underpinning a significant share of the world's chocolate industry. Abidjan is West Africa's largest French-speaking urban agglomeration and a major regional commercial and financial hub. Traditional Ivorian music includes coupé-décalé (an internationally recognized Abidjan-born urban dance music genre) and zouglou, which spread through the African diaspora. The Taï National Park (UNESCO) protects one of Africa's last remaining large tropical rainforests with chimpanzee populations. Ivorian cuisine includes attiéké (fermented cassava couscous), kedjenou (slow-braised chicken), and aloco (fried plantain). Traditional Akan goldweight art and Dan masquerade masks are internationally collected African art forms.
